resources.string: This address is on a public list of reported sites (%1$s).
This content is a program or a command (%1$s:), not a web page. It could run code.
The address contains an invisible character that reverses reading direction, so it may display differently from what it really is.
The link contains an invisible character that reverses reading direction, so part of it may display differently from what it really is.
The address looks like %1$s but uses look-alike characters that imitate other letters.
The address looks like %1$s but is spelled slightly differently.
The address contains or imitates the name of %1$s inside a longer name.
The name %2$s mixes several alphabets (%1$s). This is a common way to imitate another site.
The name %2$s is written entirely in the %1$s alphabet but reads as ordinary Latin letters. This is a common way to imitate another site.
The address contains an “@”: what comes before it is not the site. The real site is %1$s.
The address is a string of numbers (%1$s) rather than a site name. Legitimate services rarely do this.
The payment details are inconsistent (%1$s). Check the beneficiary before any transfer.
This crypto address fails its built-in check: it is mistyped or forged. Funds sent to it may be lost.
This code adds a two-factor account (%1$s). A legitimate service only shows it while you are setting it up yourself.
This two-factor code uses unusual settings (%1$s). Legitimate services rarely do this.
This number contains “*” or “#”: it is a command code (%1$s) that the dialer would run, not a phone number.
%1$s looks like a premium-rate number: calling or texting it can cost much more than usual.
%1$s is a premium-rate number in some countries. Check the cost before calling or texting.
%1$s is a very short number, often a paid service. Check the cost before calling.
This SMS goes to a short number (%1$s), often a paid service.
The text of the SMS is already written. Read it before sending it: LookFirst sends nothing.
The email has a ready-made text or a hidden recipient (bcc). Read it before sending it: LookFirst sends nothing.
The number uses digits from another writing system, which can hide the real number.
This link aims at a device of your network (box, router) or at a name that does not exist on the Internet.
This shortened link hides its real destination.
The connection is not encrypted (http): what you type can be read by others.
The address is very long: the site name is buried in the rest.
The address uses an unusual port (%1$s).
The address is not written the way a browser expects (missing scheme, unusual slashes or backslashes). It may be read differently from what is shown.
The site name is written with “%%” codes, which a site name never needs. This hides the name from a reader.
The address is malformed (empty or too long name, forbidden characters, invalid port or spaces). Different apps may read it differently.
This Wi-Fi network has no password: anyone can observe what you do on it.
This network uses WEP, an encryption that is broken: others nearby can read what you do on it.
The security type of this network was not recognised. Check it before you connect.
This code opens an app (%1$s:), not a site. LookFirst does not open it.
An app other than the browser may open this link.
No reputation list is installed: the address was not compared with reported sites.
The reputation lists could not be read: the address was not compared with reported sites.
The content could not be fully analysed: some checks were not made.
This content could not be understood. It is shown as is.
This link redirects to an unencrypted address (%1$s).
This link redirects to an address on a local or reserved network (%1$s). LookFirst did not contact it.
This link points to an address on a local or reserved network (%1$s). LookFirst did not contact it.
This link chains too many redirects or loops: LookFirst stopped following it.
The registry does not know this domain name: nothing can be said about its age.
